 Contact Lens Solution Recall: How FDA Announces, Classifies and Lists Them 
 Guide Laboratory Equipment & Instrumentation Contact Lens Solution Recall: How FDA Announces, Classifies and Lists Them
 How a contact lens solution recall is announced, classed I-III and listed by FDA, with a field-by-field guide to a recall record.
 Written and maintained by CASRAI Editorial Board 
 Last updated 1 November 2026 
 X 
 LinkedIn 
 Facebook 
 Copy link 
 Short answer
 A contact lens solution recall is a removal or correction of a lens care product that a company carries out, usually on its own initiative, and that FDA then classifies as Class I, II or III by health risk. FDA publishes the details in its Medical Device Recall Database and the weekly Enforcement Report. To check one, match the lot or code information in the record against the stock you hold. This page is general product and regulatory information, not medical advice.
 Definition and scope
 In the United States, contact lens care products are regulated as medical devices. FDA’s classification database lists, for example, Products, Contact Lens Care, Rigid Gas Permeable as a class 2 device under 21 CFR 886.5918 (openFDA device classification, checked 1 November 2026). That is why a lens solution problem is handled through the medical device recall system rather than as a general consumer-goods notice.
 FDA describes a device recall as an action usually taken by a company, whether manufacturer, distributor or other responsible party, on its own. FDA has legal authority to require a recall but has seldom needed to use it (FDA, “What is a Medical Device Recall?”, checked 1 November 2026). Under 21 CFR 7.3, a regulatory “recall” is a firm’s removal or correction of a marketed product that FDA considers violative; a market withdrawal or stock recovery is defined separately and is not a recall in that sense. For the wider device-safety vocabulary, including how the EU term fits, see field safety corrective action (FSCA) .
 How a lens solution recall is announced and listed
 There is no single notice. FDA describes several places where recall information appears:
 The Medical Device Recall Database , where FDA publishes recall details. FDA updates an entry after the recall is classified and again when the recall ends.
 The weekly Enforcement Report , in which recalls appear.
 The Medical Device Recalls and Early Alerts list, which carries the most serious recalls and early alert communications, ordered by the date FDA posts them. Listed statuses include “Recall Confirmed” and “Early Alert – FDA collecting information” (FDA, checked 1 November 2026).
 Consumer information, which FDA posts for Class I recalls and for some Class II and III recalls.
 Because only some recalls get consumer-facing posts, the database record, not a news headline, is the document to check against.
 Recall classes
 FDA assigns the class, not the recalling firm. The definitions below are FDA’s own wording.
 Class 
 FDA definition 
 Class I 
 A situation where there is a reasonable chance that a product will cause serious health problems or death. 
 Class II 
 A situation where a product may cause a temporary or reversible health problem, or where there is a slight chance that it will cause serious health problems or death. 
 Class III 
 A situation where a product is not likely to cause any health problem or injury. 
 Source: FDA, “What is a Medical Device Recall?”, checked 1 November 2026. For a side-by-side reading of the classes, see FDA recall classification: Class I vs. II vs. III .
 Reading an FDA recall record
 FDA recall records in the database share a set of fields. The list below is taken from a published record for a contact lens recall (a lens, not a solution), used here only to show the structure (FDA recall record, checked 1 November 2026).
 Field in the record 
 What to compare it with 
 Recall Status 
 Where the recall stands. The example shows “Open, Classified”; FDA updates the entry when the recall ends. 
 Product Classification 
 The class (1, 2 or 3) FDA assigned. 
 Product and Code Information 
 The product name and the lot or code scope. Match these against labels on the bottles you hold. The example’s scope reads “All distributed lenses”, so some records cover everything distributed rather than named lots. 
 Recalling Firm/Manufacturer 
 Who initiated the action, to match against your supplier and distributor records. 
 Reason for Recall and FDA Determined Cause 
 What was wrong and what FDA found to be the cause. 
 Action 
 What the firm told recipients to do. 
 Distribution and Quantity in Commerce 
 Where the product went and how much. 
 Date Initiated by Firm and Date Posted 
 Two different dates: when the firm began and when FDA published. In the example they are months apart (initiated 20 March 2024, posted 5 July 2024). 
 Recall Number and Recall Event ID 
 Identifiers to quote when you log or report a match. 
 Where it matters for labs, clinics and supply decisions
 For staff who hold lens care solution, a recall check is a records exercise. The checklist below combines FDA’s published sources with the record fields above; each step is an editorial reading of those sources, not an FDA procedure.
 Search the Medical Device Recall Database and the recalls-and-early-alerts list for the product name and manufacturer.
 Note the class, status and the “Date Posted”, and re-check later, since FDA updates entries after classification and at close.
 Compare the Code Information with the lot or code printed on your stock and in your receiving records.
 Compare Distribution with the supplier and the dates you received product.
 Record the recalling firm’s stated Action and the recall number with your records.
 Problems with a lens care product can be reported to FDA through the MedWatch program (1-800-FDA-1088) or the “Report a Problem with an FDA Regulated Product” form (FDA, checked 1 November 2026). The date on a notice matters in practice: the reasons and lots in one recall do not carry over to another product.
 Related pages: RGP contact lens solution , contact lens expiration dates , and daily vs. monthly contact lenses .
 Common misunderstandings
 “A recall means FDA ordered it.” FDA says a company usually recalls on its own; FDA has authority to require a recall but has seldom needed it.
 “Every recall is dangerous.” FDA’s classes run from Class I (serious harm or death reasonably likely) to Class III (not likely to cause any health problem or injury).
 “Recalled means the whole brand.” A record’s Code Information defines the scope; some records name specific codes and others cover everything distributed.
 “The record is final when first posted.” FDA updates the entry after classification and again when the recall ends.
 FAQ
 Who decides a contact lens solution recall?
 Usually the company that makes or distributes the product. FDA classifies the recall and publishes it.
 Where does FDA list recalls?
 In the Medical Device Recall Database, the weekly Enforcement Report, and the Medical Device Recalls and Early Alerts page.
 How do I report a problem with a lens solution?
 Through FDA’s MedWatch program at 1-800-FDA-1088 or the FDA report-a-problem form.
